column2: Act Eight
A Sigh on the River Cam
Sigh on the River Cam

“But I still cannot allow the dragons to destroy all this. If they destroy Cambridge, I will have nowhere left to remember. If they destroy Cassell College, I will have betrayed the trust of my friends in the Lionheart Society. If they destroy the graves of the girls I loved in secret, I will fight them with my life. Because these last things that give my life meaning... elusive as reflections shimmering in the light... are all I have left!”

Hands in his pockets, Anjou hummed an aria as he walked through the VIP passage of the municipal opera house. Paintings lined both sides of the narrow corridor, from Van Gogh and Monet to Rubens. Sunlight fell on the scarlet ceiling, walls, and floor, making their magnificent color flow somewhere between blood and roses.
“Congratulations on winning what you wanted.” The mild greeting sounded as if it came from an old friend.

Anjou stopped. The shadow of a small figure fell on the floor, back hunched, leaning on a cane. He looked down at it in silence for a long time. At the end of the passage, Lu Mingfei waited for him. Two security guards stood behind the boy with a cart; in its black hard case lay the set of alchemical blades worth a hundred million dollars.
Anjou smiled and waved to Lu Mingfei. “An old friend wants a word. I'll see you outside in a little while.”
Lu Mingfei left. Anjou took a deep breath but did not turn around.
“I thought you were willing to talk. Why not come in and sit down?” the man behind him asked.
“In 1899, in Texas, you shot me the instant I turned around. Ever since, I've hated hearing you call me from behind. Henkel, do you still carry that pair of alchemical revolvers?”

“It's been a hundred years. Surely you aren't still holding a grudge?” The man behind him chuckled kindly. “Back then you could only slow time for four seconds. Now it's more than ten, isn't it? You can slow a bullet in flight. What have you to worry about? Besides, I'm old too. I'm not 'Quick-Hand Henkel' anymore.”
“Your Holy Judgment is a nuisance, though. I'm still not sure I could escape your judgment.”
“We're living in modern society. We don't settle things with Yanling and alchemical revolvers anymore. Come in for a drink. Everyone's here.”

Anjou turned slowly. A crimson door hidden in the wall at the side of the corridor stood open. A gaunt old man in round glasses and a rolled-brim leather hat nodded to him. He looked like a retired Texas Ranger; a worn badge still adorned his hat.

Inside stood thirteen high-backed leather chairs, each occupied by a handsome young man. They greeted Anjou in the same way, raising their right fists to show silver rings on their index fingers: heavy, plain rings with different totems on their enormous faces. Each was a family crest.

“No introductions necessary, I suppose? Hilbert Jean Anjou, a well-known patron in our circles, a major customer, and principal of Cassell College.” Henkel sat down at the table and invited Anjou to take any seat. “How many years has it been since we spoke, Anjou?”

“The last time was December seventh, 1941, at Pearl Harbor. We were halfway through negotiations when the air-raid sirens interrupted us. The damned Japanese chose that day to bomb the place.” Anjou took an empty chair and lit a cigar.
“Yes, I remember. World War II, America declaring war, our negotiations for an alliance suspended.” Henkel nodded wistfully. “And that suspension lasted more than half a century.”
“Are these your generation's family representatives?” Anjou surveyed the well-dressed young men.

Henkel nodded. “The finest young people from each family. Some of the old fellows of our generation are dead. Others lie in hospital beds with oxygen tubes down their throats. Their bloodlines are a tragedy: they don't die suddenly of disease, only suffer slow organ failure... Their genes are imperfect, after all. They're only half dragon.” Henkel sighed. “I'm old too. I envy you, still as vigorous as a young man. If you went to a bar, young girls would still fall for such a handsome old gentleman, wouldn't they? I rather like the Maserati you drove here.”
“Don't circle around it.” Anjou puffed smoke. “We see one another at auctions, but we haven't struck up a conversation in over half a century. Why make an exception today?”
“To celebrate your winning what you wanted.” Henkel took champagne from an ice bucket, poured a glass, and handed it to Anjou.
“Thank you for withdrawing and letting us have it.” Anjou raised his glass.

“To tell the truth, we rather regret it. You wanted it so badly you brought people to disrupt the sale. It must have exceptional value. But we lost our judgment at the time. Your Mr. Lu was too clever by half, bidding like a madman. By the time we realized he was a plant you'd brought along, the auction was over.”
“A plant? He's one of our outstanding S-rank students.” Anjou smiled.

“Oh, S-rank? You have another S-rank student after all these years? You must have recruited many young people with first-rate bloodlines.” Henkel paused. “I hear you even killed Bronze and Fire, one of the Four Monarchs.”
“You've always been well informed.” Anjou studied the stemmed glass in his hand, where the wine rippled pale gold.
“But we don't know whether you obtained the dragon bones.” Henkel raised an eyebrow.

“No.” Anjou shrugged. “We could have, but something went wrong. A student acted in an emergency and struck him head-on with a Shkval torpedo. We searched the entire area afterward and found no remains.”

The young men exchanged surprised glances. They had remained wary of Anjou, resolved to listen more than they spoke. The principal of Cassell College, one of the earliest members of the Lionheart Society, the man who organized the slaughter of Dragon Kings from behind the scenes... Such an old man should have been a sharp blade; anyone reaching for its edge had to be prepared to bleed. Dragon bones were a sensitive subject, taboo even among hybrids, usually discussed under a name like the Holy Grail. When Henkel asked, the room grew tense and the young men fixed their eyes on Anjou. They would not have been surprised if the improper question made the old man turn hostile. Yet Anjou looked utterly accommodating, chatting freely about Cassell College's highest secret.
“But you confirmed that he died,” one young man said.

“No. Even one of the Four Monarchs is still a living creature, though. A direct hit from a Shkval would punch through a cruiser; his chances of survival are slim,” Anjou said mildly. “We did, however, kill Constantine and obtain his remains.”

“Congratulations.” Henkel raised his glass. “For the first time in history, we have truly killed one of the Four Monarchs. For thousands of years, the Dragon Kings' ability to form cocoons has been a nightmare for us, and you've solved that technical problem. In the foreseeable future, I believe the Dragon Kings will fall one by one. The day all Four Monarchs are buried will be the most important day in human history. Gentlemen, a toast to our compatriots.”
The young men rose together, raising their champagne. “To a new history!”
“No. What matters isn't a new history... but the end of one part of the old.” Anjou raised his glass too.
Everyone drained their glasses.
“Then, at such an important moment, might we resume negotiations for an alliance?” A young man stood. He wore a small, artistic mustache and smiled warmly.
“The door to negotiation is always open. If the terms are good enough, we'll climb the wall even if there isn't a door.” Anjou smiled.

“I admire your openness, Mr. Anjou. Had Frost Gattuso come today instead, we might not be able to sit together like friends, have a drink, and talk things over.” The young man looked into Anjou's eyes. “I think you know why.”

“The Gattuso family is the strongest among us, and Frost is its representative. He's always been hard-line. If he were here, he wouldn't give you a chance to ask questions.” Anjou spread his hands. “I'm a moderate. Everyone likes moderates.”

“Exactly. That's why we can talk. Among our compatriots, the Secret Party are the most radical, like a flock of fighting rams, and Frost is the one most fond of jumping about. We don't want to talk to him; that would be unwise.” The young man was condescending yet coaxing. A Harvard Business School graduate, he was the best negotiator among them. Speaking gently, he circled Anjou to convey his goodwill, while standing forced Anjou to look up at him. Negotiating psychology taught him that looking up at an opponent naturally placed one at a disadvantage.

“We're all hybrids. We ought to be good friends. We merely disagree on how to deal with dragons, and that difference can be bridged. We're delighted that you now have the power to kill a first-generation dragon. Dragons are our enemies too, after all. We look forward to your bringing their history to an end, and we would be glad to help.” The young man smiled.
“So generous?” Anjou raised an eyebrow.

“We're willing to give generously to our common cause, but we expect a reasonable return. When the dragons' history ends, the new age will belong to all hybrids. No single group should become the absolute leader. We should share power.” The young man rested a hand on the back of Anjou's chair, so familiar that his breath brushed Anjou's face. “If Cassell is willing to discuss sharing power, we certainly won't be stingy about helping our friends.”
Anjou shrugged. “Are we talking about dividing territory?”

“No, not dividing it. Sharing it. We're far superior to humans and ought to rule, but for all these years we've concealed our identities so carefully because the shadow of the dragons remained, haven't we? They could return at any moment and kept us in constant fear. We didn't want dragons and humans to see us as enemies at once. But now we've finally found a way to kill Dragon Kings. We're about to escape that shadow. Nothing will constrain us anymore; our influence will spread across the world! This will be our most glorious age!” The young man sounded like a Wall Street junk-bond broker, persuasive and lyrical. “Let us build that glorious age together!”
“That sounds rather good... but it's still only an ideal. Do you have a concrete plan?” Anjou asked.
“Of course.” The junk-bond broker had found a prospective client; his face lit up. “First, and most important, the Holy Grail... I mean the dragon bones... you can't keep them all to yourselves.”
“No monopoly? How about making a specimen of them and sending it on a world tour?” Anjou smiled.

“You know what I mean, Principal. Dragon bones are valuable as more than specimens for studying dragons. They contain a Dragon King's power. Dragons have only two ways to pass on power: producing offspring or devouring their own kind!” The young man circled Anjou slowly. “African cannibals believe eating a brave enemy gives them his courage. For dragons, devouring their own kind truly means inheriting an enemy's power!”
“Then split them in two, half for you and half for us. Charcoal-grilled dragon bones?” Anjou nodded and smiled. “I recommend a full-bodied California red with this reptile dish!”
“Leaving aside that unfunny joke, you're right.” The young man was losing patience. “Our condition is that you get half the dragon bones and we get half.”
“Could our half be a little bigger? We did more work, and we have a lot of students. Grilling won't stretch far enough; perhaps we'll have to make soup, one spoonful each.”
“We're expressing a sincere desire to cooperate, not haggling!” The young man was plainly angry.

“We are haggling,” Anjou said mildly. “We may all be hybrids, but for centuries we alone have fought the dragons. Our companions who emigrated to the Americas built a school, made weapons, gathered intelligence, and searched for ruins. That is how Cassell College came into being. Meanwhile, you carried gold stolen from Native Americans back to Europe, made it into jewelry for whores, danced and flirted with them, and bought property for your families. Your businesses grew larger and larger. For this war, we have lost enough companions to fill Santa Monica Beach with white crosses. After paying so much, of course we must haggle.”
Henkel coughed softly, breaking the deadlock.

“All right, all right.” The young man took a deep breath, suppressed his displeasure, and put his gentle smile back on. “We're happy to acknowledge the Secret Party's great sacrifices and will pay a reasonable price for them.”
“How reasonable?” Anjou seemed interested.

The young man sensed hope; his smile grew warmer and more enticing. “The entire hybrid community will welcome you. Trade routes across the world will be open to you. Our families will intermarry to strengthen our bloodlines and produce superior descendants. Most importantly, we will give your dragon-slaying plan our unreserved support. With the Secret Party alone, every encounter with a Dragon King is a life-or-death challenge. With us joining you, I wouldn't say victory is assured, but wouldn't your chances increase enormously?” He paused. “And for you personally... We know that although you're principal of Cassell College, you aren't the most powerful member of its Board of Trustees. Some people are dissatisfied with you, but they're only jealous because you're so outstanding. If you advance our proposal on the board and secure its approval, we'll send representatives with a substantial donation to join the board and support you wholeheartedly. At Cassell College, you unquestionably deserve to hold all the power.”
The young man studied Anjou's face. Anjou showed no expression.

Determined to strike the strongest note of the negotiation, he patted the back of Anjou's chair. “Look forward, Principal! We honor our dead friends, but we shouldn't set too high a price on the dead. History is a wheel of steel. Some people are bound to be crushed beneath it; that's their personal tragedy, but history makes it inevitable! We can't remain submerged in grief. The greatest tribute we can pay them is to enjoy the peaceful life they brought us. When the future is about to begin, why keep dwelling on the disagreements of the past? Once dragons are extinct, hybrids will stand at the top of the evolutionary tree. Humans cannot compare with us.” The young man drew a deep breath. “We will become... the new dragons!”
“New... dragons?” Anjou nodded slightly.

He lowered his head, closed his eyes, and began humming a song as if lost in thought. The young men waiting for his answer were taken aback, but recognized the aria 'The Magic of the Rhinegold' from Wagner's The Ring of the Nibelung. The dwarf Alberich admired the magically powerful gold at the bottom of the Rhine, but the three maidens guarding it mocked his ugliness and ambition without mercy. Enraged, he stole the gold and forged a ring symbolizing power, condemning himself to lose happiness as well.

The next instant, something unbelievable happened to the young man. His black suit and white shirt burst into hundreds of strips that scattered in every direction. His muscular body was entirely exposed, save for a stiffly starched collar.

Those watching Anjou saw something stranger still. Anjou, who had been sitting calmly, vanished. The champagne glass he had raised remained suspended in the air for an instant, then fell and shattered, splashing golden wine across the floor.
In the next instant, the naked young man sat in the high-backed chair, looking around in bewilderment, like someone waiting for a barber to shave him.

His barber stood behind the chair. Anjou spun a folding knife about twenty centimeters long in his hand, its edge flashing beneath the young man's jaw. Wild, beautiful patterns, characteristic of Damascus steel, covered the blade. He was still humming 'The Magic of the Rhinegold.'

The young man dared not move. Their positions had been exchanged, reversing the advantage of height. The pressure weighed like a mountain, pinning him to the chair; he lacked the strength to move a finger. His neatly trimmed mustache drifted down in the breeze. At the same time he heard his skin split with terrifying clarity. The cut grew longer, crossing his face, and a line of blood slowly appeared.
“I've wanted to trim your mustache ever since you started talking.” Anjou smiled. “But I drew blood by accident, so I won't charge you.”
“Now, Anjou, don't be angry with the child,” Henkel said mildly.

Anjou drew on his cigar. “Someone must teach him. You know I'm an educator. Young man, don't you realize you're a dwarf in the eyes of pure-blooded dragons? You carry their blood, but not all of it. You talk big and feel inferior inside. New dragons? Don't make me laugh. You only mean to steal the gold.” He blew smoke in the young man's face. “Your speech about history was splendid. Yes, great men don't care when certain people die, because their vision is broader. When I studied at Trinity College, my teacher also said those who hold power must view history from a higher place, like watching a battle from a mountain. People trample one another to death like ants, but you feel no pain because they're too far away. You're so elegant, not a spot of blood on your sleeves. How handsome! But I can't do it. I'm not on the mountaintop; I'm on that battlefield. Every second people die around me. Their pain surrounds me. I see their faces, their blood, their broken bodies, and every face is familiar. They're my companions. Henkel, I've never been a calm man, have I?”
“No,” Henkel said mildly. “You're just cool.”
“Then I'm already mad with killing. Can you lecture a man like that about the wheel of history?”
“No,” Henkel agreed.

“Henkel, I suggest you teach your children some plain truths about life. Tell them the Wall Street approach doesn't work on a desperate man mad with killing. If you want to name a price to me, first understand who I am. Don't tell me not to set too high a price on the dead, as if I were a ghoul trading in corpses. And don't talk to me about 'new dragons.' All dragons, born or self-proclaimed, are my enemies!” Anjou flicked the ash from his cigar. “Anyone who has been my enemy has come to a bad end.”
“Still, I agree with your assessment of Frost. He is a fighting ram who likes to jump about. You've learned your rhetoric well.” He patted the young man's handsome, wooden face and went out the door.
The room fell deathly silent. Only the ticking of the wall clock could be heard.

The young men all came from distinguished hybrid families, the elite of a new generation and spokesmen for their houses. Their sight and hearing were far keener than humans'. Some were natural marksmen, able to hit a target over a kilometer away with an ordinary military rifle and no optical sight. Yet none had seen what had just happened. A piece of time seemed to have been cut out of Anjou's movements: one instant he sat calmly, the next his folding knife spun in his hand. During that missing interval, one of them had lost the artistic little mustache he had cultivated for years.

Given nothing but a folding knife, how long would it take to shave off a mustache? Half a minute at least. Then... Anjou had stolen half a minute from them. How many times could a man thrust a knife in half a minute? Thirteen would be no problem, enough to kill them all!

A piercing chill lingered at the throat of the man who had lost his mustache. He clutched his neck and gasped. Everyone's shirt was soaked in cold sweat. They sat frozen, struggling to recall the instant time had been severed and the scorching majesty that had burst from Anjou, a spontaneous domain born as his bloodline burned. Ancient legends said a dragon slayer must not look a dragon in the eye: meeting such a creature's gaze would shatter the mind of anyone whose will was weak, even destroy their soul.
Dragon's majesty!

Henkel dipped a handkerchief in the ice bucket and handed it to the wounded young man. “Wipe your face. It's all right. I didn't expect you to reach an agreement with him. I only wanted to sound him out. You did well.”
“Oh. Oh.” The young man took the handkerchief in alarm and pressed it to his face. Icy water and blood ran down together, staining his shirt cuff red.
“It seems we were rash to propose cooperation so abruptly. The Secret Party is strongly opposed,” another young man said.

“Not necessarily. Cassell College does need our help. With their strength alone, they have too little chance against the Four Monarchs. But remember this lesson: with Hilbert Jean Anjou, you may negotiate and joke, but don't try to cross his bottom line.” Henkel turned to the wounded man.
“His bottom line?”

“Don't offend his dead companions.” Leaning on his cane, Henkel got laboriously to his feet. “Anjou is over a hundred and thirty, isn't he? A man that age should have his coffin ready and be listening peacefully to his grandchildren's stories. Yet when he sat calmly before me drinking champagne, I felt his body was taut, ready to spring at any moment, like a crocodile about to hunt.” He opened a drawer and took out two old-fashioned golden revolvers. He removed a round and laid it on the table: a .5-inch Magnum pistol cartridge. Even unmodified, it could knock down a hippopotamus with one shot, and this bullet's tip bore the mysterious patterns of an alchemical weapon.
The alchemical revolvers: Texas Dawn.

The young men exchanged looks, realizing they had treated Anjou far too casually. Henkel had not taken out this pair of alchemical revolvers, which had once written hybrid history, in many years. He was now a family leader of exceptional standing among hybrids; using force had long since ceased to be his job. Yet when he met Anjou, he remained armed at all times.

“I can't help being cautious face-to-face with him. We're about the same age, but I'm so old I'm nearly dead, while he's full of life like a young man. Why? Science tells us a person's age depends on the desires in his heart. A movie star in his fifties looks dashing and acts impulsively like a young man, while an office worker of the same age grows a bigger belly by the day and prepares to retire. Movie stars have greater desires. Desire keeps people young.” Henkel paused. “Anjou's desire... is revenge. That desire is more vigorous than any other, like a poisonous seed that takes root in the heart and grows into a tree until its shadow covers the whole heart.”
“How I envy his youth,” Henkel murmured, turning the alchemical revolvers in his hands, “and that desire... like a wildfire.”
“So we're just... letting it go?” a young man broke the silence.

“We'll watch and wait for now. We still have a basis for negotiating with Anjou. He's different from Frost Gattuso. Frost takes pride in the noble Gattuso bloodline and looks down on all the other families. Naturally he won't lower himself to negotiate with us. But Anjou... he only wants revenge on the dragons for his dead companions. For a hatred that has lasted a hundred years, he might agree to any terms.” Henkel smiled. “Besides, Frost is pressing him from behind. I hope Frost pushes him out even harder; then he'll drive Anjou over to our side.”
Henkel went to the wall and knocked. “Anjou has gone. Come out.”

A small red door concealed in the wall opened, and someone stepped out without a sound. A silver-gray suit, gleaming leather shoes, a rose-gold watch: the luxury suited his muscular build perfectly. The young men all looked at his feet. His steps were firm but light, with a powerful sense of rhythm. What a confident entrance! It perfectly expressed the image of a successful, elegant man; he could have replaced Sean Connery as the face of Louis Vuitton travel bags.
He sat opposite Henkel without greeting anyone. He entered this gathering of hybrid family leaders as though no one else were there.
Henkel looked up at him. “Next time, could you appear before me looking respectable?”
“A custom Prada suit, Hermès shoes, a Zenith watch.” The guest shrugged. “That should do it, shouldn't it?”
“What is that over your head?”
“You've never seen a KFC paper bag? Come on...” The man pushed a ketchup-covered fry into his mouth.
A KFC takeout bag covered his head, with two eyeholes and a mouth hole cut into it. That was why the young men could only look at his feet.

“This time you're Colonel Sanders? Last time we met at a bank and you had a black stocking over your face... The time before that was Halloween, and you wore a Darth Vader mask.” Henkel pressed a hand to his forehead. “How much do you love playing games? Can't you be professional?”
“A more professional disguise? Do you like Count Dracula? I'm in touch with several prominent vampire fan clubs in London.”
Henkel was silent for a long time. He poured a glass of strong tequila and handed it to the guest. “Actually, I prefer Cleopatra. If you don't mind, next time come naked and covered in gold powder.”

“I never imagined a man your age had such exotic tastes!” The guest chuckled. “All right, I was eating KFC takeout and borrowed the bag. It isn't time to show my face yet, is it? It wouldn't benefit either of us.”
“Everyone allowed into this room can be trusted.”
“When in history has an intelligence leak come from anyone but someone trusted?”
Henkel paused. “You have a point. You heard what Anjou said. Should we believe him, especially about the dragon bones?”

“It sounds as though he concealed nothing. He has one set of dragon bones. There should have been two, but the other sank in the Three Gorges Reservoir and couldn't be recovered. The Board of Trustees has asked for the bones, but Anjou hasn't handed them over.”

“So many people are interested in dragon bones.” Henkel smiled. “But apart from using them to make the Philosopher's Stone, nobody knows their true value, do they? They supposedly contain a Dragon King's power, but how does one open that treasure house?”
“If no one has the key, all you can do is dig up the whole treasure house and bury it in your own backyard, so you'll be first when the day comes that it can be opened.”
“Where is their next target?”

The man shook his head. “No definite news. But the Executive Department has clearly been very active lately. The latest word is that a top-secret document has just arrived at the college from China, only to be sent straight on to the Board of Trustees. The next target is probably in China too. They've consistently promoted Chinese-language education and trained a team fluent in Chinese. That can't have been just for the Three Gorges operation.”
“China? Keep watching, then.” Henkel nodded. “I'm also very interested in Lu Mingfei.”
“An utterly ordinary freshman, now a sophomore, in the throes of a troublesome adolescence. His luck has always been good, and what he needs most at present is a girlfriend.”

“Does he have a special background? Something incredible happened at the auction. Before he entered, his account held only two million in collateral. Yet he boldly bid up to twenty million. We had to suspend the auction and check his ability to pay. The first check still showed only two million. When he requested a second... in ten seconds his balance shot up to a hundred and two million dollars. He immediately raised the price to a hundred million and bought the alchemical blades. After the hammer fell, Cassell College transferred a hundred million to us. Remember, the payment did not come from Lu Mingfei's account. But when we checked his account then, it held only two million again.” Henkel was silent for a moment. “As if someone had advanced him a hundred million in collateral exactly when he needed it!”
“Was the bank's computer system hacked? Or Anjou advanced the hundred million. Anjou can still command that much money.”

Henkel shook his head. “Neither. The computer system was entirely normal, and Cassell College didn't back Lu Mingfei. The people who supported him were an enormous crowd: individual stock investors. In those ten seconds, twenty-five million retail investors in markets from the Americas to Europe and Asia each transferred four dollars from their accounts to Lu Mingfei, totaling a hundred million. After the auction, the money automatically went back. In other words, when he needed money, the whole world donated to him, twenty-five million streams of cash converging on him; when he didn't need it, the money returned automatically. Its withdrawal caused the indices of the world's major stock markets, from the Dow Jones Industrial Average to London's Financial Times index, to fall 0.000001 percent simultaneously, in exchange for Lu Mingfei's instant fortune.”

The man thought for a long time, then shook his head. “It sounds more like a hacker, but breaking into twenty-five million retail accounts worldwide would require enormous server resources. I don't think any hacker group in the world has that technology.”
“No, it wasn't like a hacker. It was like... the hand of God... shifting the balance of wealth.” Henkel spoke softly. “Make monitoring Lu Mingfei a priority from now on.”

“Understood. If there's nothing else, I'll be going.” The man played with his glass of tequila. A curled butterfly larva floated in the brown liquor. “Henkel, you must have been one incredibly cool cowboy back then. Even your choice of liquor is so Western.”
“From the town of Tequila, made from genuine blue agave. Top quality.” Henkel pushed a silver dish of fine salt and lemon slices toward him. “Try it.”
“If I'd known there'd be drinking, I'd have dressed as Zorro,” the man said regretfully. “Colonel Sanders is rather inconvenient.”

He carefully tore the mouth hole in the bag wider, deftly sprinkled salt on the web between his left thumb and forefinger, picked up a slice of lemon, and raised the glass in his right hand. Gazing at the curled larva in the brown liquor, he took a deep breath. “A real man's drink!”
He sucked the lemon, licked the salt clean, and threw back his head. The entire glass of tequila went down, after which he spat the worm into the silver dish with a loud, forceful sound.
“Ah!” He wriggled with pleasure. “Like a fireball rolling into my stomach!”

“You do love performing. Now turn into a ball and roll out of here, and don't forget to close the door,” Henkel said mildly. “And a reminder: you'd better find something else to cover your face. Your bag is about to tear.”
“How could that defeat me?” The guest turned the bag, moving the tear to the back of his head and bringing the intact rear side over his face.
“See you next time, Sheriff Henkel.” He rose, gave an awkward imitation of a Texas Ranger's salute, and turned to leave.
With a bang, he walked into the doorpost.
“Forgot to cut eyeholes... damn it!” he muttered, feeling his way out.
Henkel stared silently out the window and began to wonder whether entrusting the future of hybrids to an idiot like that was courage or insanity.
The Maserati raced down the highway with its hardtop open. An old man and a young one wore sunglasses as sunshine and wind poured over their faces.
“Give this to the Academic Affairs Committee. They'll excuse you from the makeup exam.” Anjou handed Lu Mingfei a hastily scribbled note.
“That's enough?” Lu Mingfei took the paper on which his GPA depended. It was just a note, without even a personal seal.
“This is special authorization from the principal.” Anjou glanced at him. “I rarely exercise this privilege, so the board won't question my fairness as an educator.”
“Principal, you look awfully serious...” Lu Mingfei cautiously studied Anjou, then glanced at the back seat, where the heavy black hard case held alchemical weapons worth a hundred million dollars.

They were like two great thieves who had stolen the Dragon-Slaying Saber, the weapon that commanded the world, from the Lion-Slaying Assembly at Shaolin Temple and were fleeing on swift horses. Shouldn't they be laughing triumphantly? Yet after an old friend called the originally excited principal away for a drink, his face had remained expressionless.

“Those people who call themselves old friends will soon become our enemies.” Anjou understood what Lu Mingfei was thinking. “If we can kill all Four Monarchs... I mean if. The day the last Dragon King falls in a pool of blood... will be the day hybrids go to war with one another.”
“War? But we're all brothers and sisters...”

“Dragons aren't very sentimental about their own kind. Though Constantine and Norton seemed to have strong brotherly affection, more dragons kill one another. Dragon blood is the strongest genetic inheritance in the history of evolution. Its nature is a struggle to the death. Only the dragons with the finest bloodlines survive, improving their genetic advantage step by step. We inherited that nature too; you just haven't noticed it yet.”
“Then I'd rather not notice. As a coward, discovering that my genes say the winner takes all would be a tragedy!”

“Can't you have a little self-respect? You're our only S-rank!” Anjou smiled helplessly. “We've already put you forward. This auction was your first step onto the hybrid social stage, and you've made a deep impression. Soon hybrid families all over the world will know that an exceptional new descendant has appeared. His name is Lu Mingfei.”
Lu Mingfei froze for a second, then bristled. “Hey! I was just a plant this time, right? A plant doesn't need everyone he tricks to remember his name, does he?”
He understood the old man's sinister intentions. This was no opportunity to make a name for himself; it was a pit of fire through and through.

Soon every reptile in the world would know Lu Mingfei was Cassell College's new ace. What did being an ace mean? Take Guan Yunchang of the Three Kingdoms, Brother Guan: famous everywhere, Liu Bei's most capable subordinate, one of the most dangerous outlaws of his day. Every outlaw in the land wanted to kill him but didn't dare. Even Cao Cao gave him a thumbs-up. He was unbelievably cool. But after decades of glory, he died, ambushed by some nobody. He had survived so long because he truly had ability. If Jiang Gan had been the ace... he wouldn't even have reached Maicheng; he'd have died crossing the five passes and slaying six generals!

Compared with Brother Guan, Lu Mingfei didn't mind admitting he was more like Jiang Gan. Jiang Gan had it good: Zhou Yu didn't kill him when he came as a persuader, and Cao Cao didn't kill him when he stole false intelligence.

No wonder the invitation carried his real name. It wasn't that the college couldn't be bothered inventing an alias. They had planned all along to use this opportunity to make the name Ricardo M. Lu known.

“Like dragons, hybrids take pride in superior bloodlines. Every family introduces its finest descendants to everyone. The more exceptional heirs it has, the more respect it receives. We finally discovered an S-rank in you, so naturally we had to put you forward,” Anjou said. “Like presenting the family's most beautiful young lady to society.”
Lu Mingfei wanted to smash his head into the airbag in front of him and make it deploy around his face.
“Principal, assigning me S-rank really wasn't just messing with me?” Lu Mingfei looked miserable.
“Of course not. I wouldn't joke about that.” Anjou gave him a meaningful look. “Your S-rank was determined from the purity of your parents' bloodlines.”

“Mom and Dad?” Something trembled quietly inside Lu Mingfei. He hadn't seen them for years. He said he expected nothing of the two unreliable people, but deep down he missed them. Whenever they came up, he couldn't keep playing the fool.
The speeding Maserati suddenly slowed. Anjou pulled into a highway rest area, lit a fresh cigar, drew deeply, and blew smoke toward the clear blue sky.
“You don't remember much about your parents, do you?” Anjou gazed into the distance.

“Not much. I was about twelve when they left home and never came back.” Lu Mingfei seemed lost in thought. “They worked at a geological institute then and traveled a lot, always for a long time, leaving me home alone. When I was little, I ate at a hundred families' tables.”
“A hundred families' tables?”
“A meal at one house, then a meal at another.”
Anjou nodded. “Did you resent them?”

“Not really. When I was little, I thought my parents traveled all over the world for work and were a hundred times cooler than anyone else's. To me they were Indiana Jones; roaming the world was what they were supposed to do... Later I realized pride doesn't put food on the table. No matter how impressive your parents are, it means nothing if they can't pick you up from school.” Lu Mingfei scratched his head.
“Indiana Jones?” Anjou smiled silently. “No. They were far more than Indiana Jones. Lu Lincheng and Qiao Weini had the purest bloodlines we had discovered before Chu Zihang... Both were S-rank.”
“No way! Didn't you say there hadn't been an S-rank student in years?” Lu Mingfei was bewildered. Three S-ranks in one family sounded like a party that could sweep any dungeon!

“Your parents only took advanced studies at Cassell College. They weren't technically students, only alumni. And their records have always been confidential; very few people know. You know that once the proportion of dragon genes exceeds human genes, a hybrid visibly undergoes dragon transformation, becoming more dragon than human. In other words, once bloodline purity passes a certain threshold, the critical blood threshold, a powerful friend can instantly become a powerful enemy. When we first discovered your parents, they resonated extremely strongly with Draconic. We were all worried their bloodline purity exceeded the critical blood threshold. You hadn't been born then, but you were already in your mother's womb. We had to decide whether to let you be born...”

“Hey! Principal, isn't that going too far? I was their first child. Even family planning wouldn't have had anything to say about me!” Lu Mingfei protested at once. He had obviously made it safely through that dangerous embryonic period, but the thought that someone had once voted on whether he should be born still frightened him. What kind of cold-blooded killers had cast those votes?
“It was a very serious vote. Before you were born, even our most experienced bloodline professors didn't know whether you would be a dragon.”
“You said... a dragon?” Lu Mingfei wondered if he'd heard wrong.

“Yes. Not a true pure-blooded dragon, but a hybrid with such a high proportion of dragon blood that they display a dragon's appearance. We also call them dragons. Usually hybrids don't have very pure dragon blood, and when they have children together, those children are human in form. But in extremely rare cases, when two hybrids with exceptionally pure dragon blood have a child, a 'purification effect' can occur. It's like the pharaohs of ancient Egypt often marrying their sisters: both possessed noble royal blood, and their offspring were believed to be more divine. Although modern genetics considers it dangerous, it is indeed possible to produce a child whose bloodline purity exceeds the critical blood threshold. In that case you would very likely show dragon characteristics...”
“I've got horns on my head... and a tail behind me?” Trembling, Lu Mingfei reached back to feel his backside.
Anjou stared. “What are you doing?”
“I remember my tailbone has stuck out a bit ever since I was little... I don't know if it's a tail that never grew in or something...”
“Can you stop talking nonsense on a serious occasion?”
“Sometimes being nervous just makes me talk more...”

Anjou shook his head. “In any case, statistically, because of your parents' highly pure bloodlines, you really might have been a dragon. Although morally it would have been cruel to destroy an unknown life, you know the Secret Party has never been particularly reasonable... The point was that we dared not risk allowing a dragon to be born, and the votes for and against were evenly divided. Finally your mother stood up. Her words, as a woman, were supremely sacred. When she spoke, her beauty as a woman astonished everyone there. She said, 'This child is the treasure of my life. If I lose him, I don't know how I can face the rest of it. I am willing to give birth alone in a sealed glass chamber, without a nurse or doctor's help. You may watch from outside. If I give birth to a dragon, you have the right to destroy both mother and child.'”
Lu Mingfei stared blankly up at the sky, imagining the woman's incomparable beauty at that moment, so beautiful that even hard-hearted men lowered their heads and dared not look directly at her.

“At the time, it seemed the least risky method. Some dragons are highly mobile before they leave the womb and can even use Yanling. Once born, they might escape before anyone could stop them, and the midwives would be their first targets. A young dragon could kill them the instant it opened its eyes,” Anjou said. “Her strength and beauty had almost persuaded us. Then a man stood up and said, 'No!'”
“Who was so inconsiderate?” Lu Mingfei felt indignant.

Anjou smiled. “Your father. He said, 'I will deliver my wife's baby. I'll start practicing the technique right now. My wife must not give birth alone!' He also said, 'I want an opaque empty chamber as the delivery room. You can strap bombs to the outside and hold the detonator at a distance. If she gives birth to a dragon, I'll sound the alarm immediately; please detonate the bombs. I can die... but I cannot allow other men to watch my wife give birth!'”
“That's my dad, all right! What a man!” Lu Mingfei was so moved he nearly cried.

Anjou patted his shoulder. “Your parents staked their lives on their insistence, and so you were finally born into this world like any other child. If you once blamed them for not taking good care of you, perhaps now you can forgive them. They were willing to do anything for you, from changing your diapers to dying for you.”
Lu Mingfei reclined in the racing seat, gazing up at the sky. After a long silence, he said, “They never told me any of that.”

“Often that's how it is. You do a great deal for the person you love most, and they don't know, because you think it's only right and forget to tell them.” Anjou breathed out smoke and sighed. “But we still couldn't rest easy. From birth you were a little white mouse under observation. We watched you for eighteen years and dispatched our finest observers.”
Lu Mingfei's eyes widened. Observers? Had such people really appeared in his life? Had mysterious agents in black suits and sunglasses followed him from childhood?
“They all had disguises. Some seemed to be teachers at your school, some people selling newspaper subscriptions door to door, some from the electric company...”
“I knew that meter reader looked shifty! He looked everywhere as soon as he came in. So he really was up to no good!” Lu Mingfei suddenly understood.

“You are our hope. Others may think I protect you in a peculiar way. But to me you're a young man worth believing in, just like exceptional descendants such as Caesar and Chu Zihang,” Anjou said. “I've watched you for eighteen years, like... Have you seen a Chinese cartoon called Calabash Brothers?”

Lu Mingfei covered his face. “Something strange has slipped into our serious conversation... Okay, I get it. You're the old man who grows the gourds. Now, crack, the gourd splits and I jump out, with the powers of acting like an idiot and playing StarCraft, and you send me off to fight monsters? But Principal, are you really sure two exceptional hybrids produce an exceptional hybrid?”
“Hmm.” Anjou considered. “It is possible the result could be a defective product, for example if you inherited all your parents' junk genes.”
“Hey... even if it's true, could you not use 'defective product'? It's bad for my self-esteem.”

“But you're not defective. Your bloodline test results were beyond first-rate. Your blood could even make the living spirit guarding the Bronze City retreat. You're the one we've been waiting for!” Anjou said. “With great power comes great responsibility.”

“Suddenly we've switched from Calabash Brothers to Spider-Man... But Principal, I really don't think I'm suited to the great work of saving the world. The bloodline test, the Bronze City and all that... were just good luck.” Lu Mingfei thought, One burst of power costs me a quarter of my life. Do you think I'm a nine-lived cat? Could this be my Yanling? Like a strange character in a game party: everyone else spends mana, but this guy's ultimate move consumes his health bar. When it's empty, he drops dead and the boss is blasted down too. The ending shows everyone laying white flowers at his gravestone while lovers confess their feelings to each other.
“Mingfei, have you ever thought about your reason for living in this world?” Anjou drew deeply on his cigar.

Lu Mingfei hesitated, then said cautiously, “If I said it was for the games I haven't played, the serials I haven't finished... and the girlfriend I haven't picked up yet... would you kick me out of the car?”
“Does the girlfriend you haven't picked up mean Chen Motong, the girl who always likes to wear red?”

“Hey! Principal! Could you not bring up the one thing I don't want to talk about? Let's go back to your deep philosophical subject! Continue with why we live in this world!” Lu Mingfei blushed and tried to stand his ground.

“Oh.” Anjou nodded, eyes distant, as if his thoughts had flown to the far end of time. “When I was at Cambridge, people's tastes were different. Girls wore long white silk dresses and Oxford-style high heels with white soles. I'd stand by the Bridge of Sighs holding a book of poetry, pretending to read while I watched the girls walk past and waited for the wind to lift their white silk skirts.” The old man blew out a thread of smoke, a look of longing on his face. “And reveal their lovely calves. Oh, heavens! Wonderful! At the time, I thought I lived for that sight!”
“Hey! What's philosophical or deep about that? You're just as bad as me!”
“But now they're all dead. Sometimes I bring a bouquet of white roses to visit their graves,” the old man said wistfully.
“Hey! How did all that tender feeling mix so naturally with the leering from a moment ago?”

The old man ignored him and went on. “I still often return to Cambridge, but there's no one on campus I know anymore, and time has erased all evidence that I once studied there. I can't exactly take out my old diploma and tell people I graduated from Cambridge Divinity School in 1897. They'd think I was mad, or a monster. When I speak with people, I say I'm only a tourist who dreamed of Cambridge when I was young. I walk alone through campus, watching students pass in T-shirts and sneakers with all kinds of handheld electronic devices. They no longer discuss poetry, religion, and art, but devote themselves to finding jobs in the City of London. And what of the things I cherished? The girls I admired? Their lovely white silk dresses and Oxford-style heels with white soles? The linden tree beneath whose shade we discussed Shelley's poems? They're all history in old photographs. I pass the young people like a lonely ghost who has traveled a hundred years.”
Anjou paused. “How do you understand blood sorrow?”

Lu Mingfei stared. Blood sorrow? He had never understood it. Guderian said hybrids lived in the human world as sadly as lost lambs, but Lu Mingfei had always thought that was nonsense. Sad about what? That ordinary people couldn't use Yanling and you could? Hilarious! If he had Caesar's Kamaitachi, he only had to prick up his ears and listen to a girl's heart rate when she spoke to him to know if she liked him. Chu Zihang's Sovereign Flame would do too: a portable gas burner. At a picnic he could hold a pan in one hand and make fried rice while using the other to heat water for tea.

What sorrow? Why be sad because you have more than other people? People are only sad when others have something they don't, aren't they? Like when someone picks everyone else up in a car on a rainy day while you pull off your clothes to cover your head and run home; or when a father and mother sit behind everyone else at a parent-teacher meeting like a pair of door gods while you have an empty white wall behind you; or when someone's whole family sees them off abroad, holding hands and gazing tearfully at one another at security, passionately embracing a girlfriend and promising to meet again in summer, while you drag a huge suitcase through the long security line alone...
Come to think of it... his life really was miserable.

He used to read The Legend of the Condor Heroes in class. When the great master Huang Yaoshi saw his disobedient daughter insist on remaining with the foolish Guo Jing, he remembered his dead wife, waved a hand and killed two fine horses, then, overcome by sorrow, chanted a famous line from the Western Han scholar Jia Yi's 'Ode to the Owl': “Heaven and earth are the furnace, creation the smith; yin and yang are the charcoal, all things the bronze.” Han Baoju, a mediocre swordsman with a considerable reputation, didn't understand and asked his brother Zhu Cong what the old fellow was on about. Zhu Cong had some education and explained that the old man meant life was an ordeal, like being roasted in a great furnace, and he was very sad. Han Baoju was contemptuous. Damn it! The old man was so powerful; what could he possibly have to be unhappy about?

Nine people out of ten would probably think Han Baoju uncultured. Only Lu Mingfei thought he was right. Old hero Huang Yaoshi was so literary and so easily saddened; would he trade places with Han Baoju if he had the chance? Han Baoju was thick-skinned and cheerful, loyal to his good brothers until he died, merely a little lacking in martial skill. If old hero Huang wouldn't trade, that meant his sadness was hypocritical.

What was this about the strongest being the loneliest? Lonely people were all putting on airs. If you always struck a lonely pose, it was because you hadn't suffered enough loneliness yet and still thought the pose looked cool.

Truly lonely people never think about it. If you're already terribly lonely and can't save yourself, all you can do is not think. But Lu Mingfei didn't yet understand that then... Late at night he sat on the rooftop, looking toward the distant lights, imagining the day he would become amazing, and grinned foolishly in silence.
Anjou lapsed into a long reverie until the cigar butt burned his hand.

“Whenever I fly over London, I look down for the River Cam, then follow it to the Bridge of Sighs... Do you know how the bridge got its name? A hundred years ago, Cambridge had a rule that students who broke college rules were punished by being made to think beside the bridge. We always sighed while we thought.” Anjou ran his tongue over his teeth, then suddenly smiled with unusual delight. “Do you think I'm contradicting myself? I lament that Cambridge is no longer what it was, yet say I'm still attached to it.”
“I didn't understand, in any case,” Lu Mingfei admitted honestly.

“Today's Cambridge is only a ghost of the Cambridge of a hundred years ago, but I still find myself returning again and again. Standing there, I still feel warm. I can faintly sense the air of a hundred years ago, and the white silk dresses and Oxford-style heels with white soles in my memory become vivid again.” Anjou spoke softly. “I have no family. My best friends are all dead. Even among hybrids I've lived to a sadly great age. There isn't much left in this world for me to cherish. What if I kill all the Dragon Kings? Will my Cambridge reappear? Will my friends come back to life? Will the girls I admired jump from their graves, divorce their husbands, who have also become bones, and come running into my arms? Wearing my favorite long white silk dresses and Oxford-style heels? Even I feel the meaning of my life has ebbed away with time. My reason for living in this world is too fragile.”

The old man drew fiercely on his cigar, sharp lines appearing at the corners of his eyes. “But I still cannot allow the dragons to destroy all this. If they destroy Cambridge, I will have nowhere left to remember. If they destroy Cassell College, I will have betrayed the trust of my friends in the Lionheart Society. If they destroy the graves of the girls I loved in secret, I will fight them with my life. Because these last things that give my life meaning... elusive as reflections shimmering in the light... are all I have left!” He forcefully spat the cigar butt out of the car. “If anyone dares touch my last piece of cream cake, how could I not fight them with my life?”
Lu Mingfei was stunned.

Damn! He'd never imagined... the old man was such a fiercely lonely man! He drove luxury cars, wore custom suits, and carried beautiful young women on his arm, attracting attention like an absurdly elderly playboy. Yet when that ferocity emerged, he was as intimidating as the folding knife he never put down.
“Mingfei, what about your reason? What fragile reason has kept you from suddenly deciding to jump off the rooftop one day while enjoying the cool air?” Anjou raised an eyebrow.
“What do you mean? Jump off?”
“Everyone has a reason to go on living. That's why we don't get high and jump off a building or something.”
“Isn't the girlfriend I haven't picked up enough?”
“Not enough!”
“Then what about Dynasty Warriors 6 and StarCraft II, which haven't come out yet?”
“Still not enough!”
“All right, I'll be serious. I really do want to see my parents again, even though they've been pretty lousy to me and haven't come back to see me for years...”
“Still not enough!” Anjou smiled mysteriously. “The meaning of life... is those things that flash through your mind when you're about to die...”

He suddenly started the engine and floored the accelerator. The Maserati reared like a shark leaping from the water, its rear tires pouring smoke against the road. Lu Mingfei and his scream were both pressed into the racing seat by the mad acceleration. This was the car at full power: in half a minute it approached four hundred kilometers per hour, a speed Caesar's Bugatti could reach. Driving at that speed on an ordinary highway was like firing an aircraft cannon shell from an old hunting rifle! The highway, previously sparsely traveled, suddenly became crowded. At that speed, passing one car meant quickly encountering the next. The Maserati swept past one vehicle after another in uncanny arcs. The terrified drivers honked behind them, their horns stretched out by the speed and rapidly left behind. To a Ferrari traveling at two hundred kilometers an hour, the Maserati passing it was like that Ferrari passing a stationary pedestrian: the relative speed was two hundred kilometers an hour!
The maniacs in the Equipment Department had tuned it! No doubt about it!
Lu Mingfei should have thought of it. Anjou's Yanling was Time Zero, which extended the effect of time. Once he activated it, this speed would be nowhere near enough, about like a bicycle.
How could a mad old man who loved driving fast and possessed that Yanling have anything but a beast that ran on the edge of losing control for a car?

But at this moment Lu Mingfei had lost the ability to reason. He couldn't count how often he thought they were about to hit the car ahead, or how often he thought a rapid lane change would throw him out. Light and shadows swirled before his eyes; his brain was starved of blood.
That old man Anjou... put on sunglasses and loudly sang some old song into the sunshine!

Wasn't this the old man's life? More than a hundred and thirty years spent always rushing generously toward death, always charging ahead at high speed without knowing when he would hit a wall and be smashed to pieces. Once accustomed to it, he could sing loudly without fear.
“Do you feel the past rushing at you, Mingfei? See that slow old Beetle ahead? We're about to hit it! Think quickly!” The old man laughed.
Damn it! He really was trying, but nothing came. His mind was blank... What moment in this trashy life was he most reluctant to leave behind?
The rooftop at Aunt's house? He had sat there in the quiet of the night, staring at a sea of lights and imagining someone would take him to see a whole new world one day. But could he still go back?
Those sunny afternoons, Chen Wenwen reading on a bench in her almost transparent white cotton dress? But what did any of that have to do with Lu Mingfei?

Nono stepping out of her diving suit beneath the Three Gorges. Oh! In a bikini, enough to give a man a nosebleed! But the girl, her magnificent figure, and even her swimsuit all belonged to the boss on the ship above!

Was there really nothing else to think about? Was his life made up of these fragments? Nothing worth clinging to. Everything he longed for or thought about was either a daydream or somebody else's girlfriend. In that case... getting drunk and jumping off a building wasn't entirely out of the question...

Suddenly a fresh, exuberant green rushed toward him like a boundless forest. Sunlight filtered through the leaves, illuminating Lu Mingfei's eyes. His pupils widened and his whole body trembled as if an electric current passed through him. Once again he saw the old house where he'd lived as a child, new tendrils of ivy covering the window, sunlight filtered green before it was allowed into the room. He was a little boy waiting for his parents to come home from work. Another little boy stood beside him, holding his head...
“Brother, you have to live,” the child said softly. “We all have to live. Life is the only... everything we have!”
Lu Mingze!

Damn it! What was going on? That was his childhood! When had this little devil invaded even that? And delivered such a corny, ridiculous, tragic line, while the two boys embraced? Damn! It made him want to puke!
But suddenly his tears began to fall, and he didn't know why.
Suddenly he was so very sad.
“Our fire... will set the whole world... alight!” Lu Mingze whispered.

The Maserati slowed gently and pulled over. The old man glanced at Lu Mingfei, handed him two tissues, and took out a fresh cigar. “Looks like you felt something! But you don't have to tell me. Everyone has a reason to live. Once you've understood it, just remember it. We fight the dragons for these fragile reasons. Fragile, yes, but they're all we have.”
Lu Mingfei wiped his face and nodded. “Damn! That was embarrassing.”

Thinking about it, it really wasn't fair. Plenty of people in the world had ten or a hundred times more than he did: houses, cars, girlfriends, wonderful lives lived to the fullest every day, not to mention bright futures. Yet a guy with nothing like him had to save the world. Shouldn't those with money give money and those with strength give strength? While he risked his life, Zhao Menghua was somewhere holding Liu Miaomiao around her slender waist. Why should he make such an effort?
But suddenly he was so, so unwilling to accept it! Our fire... will set the whole world... alight?
